sections.h2: How do you reach the Guernsey County Recorder in Cambridge?
sections.html:
The Guernsey County Recorder is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The phone is 740-432-9275 and the fax is 740-439-6267, according to the county recorder page. The auditor's office is in the Administration Building at 627 Wheeling Avenue in Cambridge, the county seat and largest city, and the recorder's contact details are on the county site.

In Ohio the recorder keeps the ownership record for land and every lien against it. Indexing each document is what lets a title examiner build a chain of title, so a seller whose deed was never recorded can expect the buyer's title company to stop the sale until it is.

sections.h2: Can a Guernsey County deed be recorded electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. The recorder accepts eRecordings from four submitting vendors, and mortgage companies, banks, attorneys and title companies are the usual users. Only document types accepted through the regular mail can be eRecorded, and the vendors set their own prices.

The auditor's page describes a second route, e-filing through Kofile Technologies. Documents can be transmitted at any hour, any day, and they are processed from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. on weekdays. Anything sent after 3:00 p.m. waits for the next business day. Plats and military discharges (DD-214) cannot be e-recorded. A rejected deed or conveyance form restarts the clock when the corrected version comes in.

sections.h2: What does the Guernsey County Auditor do before a deed is recorded?
sections.html:
The auditor's real estate staff transfer the deed on the tax records, then send it to the recorder. The auditor is at 627 Wheeling Avenue, Suite 301, and the phone is (740) 432-9243, option 1 for real estate. Its forms list for sellers and closing agents includes:

  • DTE 100, the real estate conveyance form, and DTE 100 EX for exempt transfers
  • DTE 101, the statement of conveyance of homestead property
  • DTE 102, the statement of conveyance of CAUV property
  • A routing sheet and a timeline for deed transfers
  • Transfer and Conveyance Standards effective October 1, 2022

A conveyance fee calculator is on the auditor's tools menu. State law sets a $1.00 per thousand fee in R.C. 319.54 and lets a county levy up to 30 cents per hundred dollars as a transfer tax under R.C. 322.02, so use the calculator or call to get the amount Guernsey County charges.

sections.h2: What do the buyer and seller sign for the Guernsey County Auditor?
sections.html:
The conveyance statement follows R.C. 319.202. The buyer, or the buyer's representative, submits it before the auditor endorses the deed. The statement states the value of the property, which means the full price including any mortgage or vendor's lien, and it is a crime to knowingly falsify that value.

The same statute asks about tax reductions and farm status:

  • An affirmation that the seller was asked whether the property's current or prior year taxes carry a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction, or a sworn statement that explains the reduction and its estimated amount.
  • An affirmation about whether the parcel qualified for the current agricultural use valuation (CAUV), or a sworn statement that mentions a possible recoupment charge.
  • The reason for any exemption, written on the form, when no fee is due.

After endorsing the deed, the auditor keeps the original statement, sends one copy to the tax commissioner and gives one to the buyer. Residential rental property carries an extra notice that the buyer must file registration information with the auditor.

sections.h2: How much does the Guernsey County Recorder charge?
sections.html:
The recorder's fees follow R.C. 317.32, and the Ohio Recorders' Association publishes the combined version: $34.00 for the first two pages, $8.00 for each added page and $4.00 for a marginal notation, with a preservation surcharge of up to $5.00 per document. The association's table notes that half of the fee is the basic recording fee and half goes to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund.

The same table lists a standardization fee of $10.00 plus $10.00 for a document that does not meet the formatting requirements. Ask the recorder at 740-432-9275 whether the county adds a surcharge, since Senate Bill 94 left that choice to each county.

sections.h2: Who may sign and notarize an Ohio deed?
sections.html:
A deed must be signed by the grantor and acknowledged before an official named in R.C. 5301.01: a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. Many Guernsey County sellers use a notary at a bank, a title company or an attorney's office.

R.C. 5301.25 requires recording in the county where the land lies, and it says an unrecorded deed is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer who bought in good faith. If a survey was done, the name of the surveyor must appear in the deed.

The auditor's delinquent tax notice cites R.C. 5721.03 and explains that listed parcels will be certified for foreclosure or a tax certificate sale unless the delinquent taxes, assessments, interest and penalties are paid within one year. A seller with a listed parcel should pay it at or before closing so the buyer's title is clear.

sections.h2: What is Guernsey County like for owners and buyers?
sections.html:
Guernsey County lies in the Appalachian foothills and was organized in 1810. It covers about 522 square miles of land, and the auditor counts 40,170 parcels. The Census Bureau estimates 38,379 residents in 2025, roughly flat since 2020, and 22.1 percent are 65 or older.

For 2020 to 2024 the median value of an owner-occupied home is $157,700, the owner-occupied rate is 72.1 percent, and median gross rent is $864. Median household income is $58,478. The county issued 41 building permits in 2025. The auditor's forms list includes a Mineral Deeds section, so ask the buyer's title company to search for any recorded mineral deed or lease on the parcel.

sections.h2: What do more Census figures show about Guernsey County?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau counts 16,318 households for 2020 to 2024, with 2.31 people per household and 19,116 housing units as of 2025. Median monthly owner costs are $1,237 with a mortgage and $505 without. About 86.4 percent of households have a broadband subscription, which is below the 92.8 percent shown for Greene County.

The county has 73.6 people per square mile, and the mean commute is 22.9 minutes. Guernsey County lost land to Noble County in 1851 when four townships changed hands, and today its adjoining counties are Tuscarawas, Coshocton, Harrison, Noble, Muskingum and Belmont. Buffalo, Kimbolton and Salesville are census-designated places beyond Cambridge, and a deed for land there is recorded in the same Cambridge office.

faqs.q: What are the Guernsey County Recorder's hours?
faqs.a: Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The office phone is 740-432-9275, and electronic filings are processed between 8:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. on weekdays.

faqs.q: Can I eRecord a deed in Guernsey County?
faqs.a: Yes, through one of four submitting vendors or through e-filing with Kofile. Plats and military discharges cannot be e-recorded, and your title company usually handles the submission.

faqs.q: Which office do I see first, the auditor or the recorder?
faqs.a: The auditor. The deed is transferred on the tax records with a conveyance form, and then it is forwarded to the recorder for recording. Ask the auditor about its deed transfer timeline.

faqs.q: How much is the base recording fee in Guernsey County?
faqs.a: The Ohio Recorders' Association table prints $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each added page, with a preservation surcharge of up to $5.00 per document. Confirm any county surcharge with the recorder.

faqs.q: What happens to a deed I never recorded?
faqs.a: Under R.C. 5301.25 it is treated as fraudulent against a later good-faith purchaser who did not know about it. Record it with the county recorder as soon as the auditor has transferred it.
